items.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault?

Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), which means your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault, but not eliminated unless you are equally or more at fault than the other party. Insurance companies often try to inflate your share of fault to reduce what they owe.

A workers' compensation claim in Georgia operates differently from every other personal injury claim. It's a no-fault system — meaning you don't have to prove your employer was negligent to receive benefits. If you were injured while performing your job duties, you are generally entitled to medical treatment and income replacement, regardless of fault.

Georgia requires most employers with three or more employees to carry workers' compensation insurance (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-2). That coverage pays for medical care and provides weekly income benefits if your injury prevents you from working. But employers and their insurers have significant financial incentives to minimize your claim, dispute your injury, or push you back to work before you're ready.

items.question: What should I do if my workers' comp claim is denied in Georgia?
items.answer: A denial is not final. In Georgia, you can file a claim with the State Board of Workers' Compensation to dispute a denial (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-100). You have the right to a hearing before an administrative law judge, and the right to appeal further if needed. The process is procedurally complex — which is why having a Georgia workers' compensation attorney from the start significantly improves your chances.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' comp claim in Georgia?
items.answer: No. Georgia law prohibits employers from retaliating against employees for filing a workers' comp claim (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11.1). Termination, demotion, reduced hours, or other adverse actions taken in response to a comp claim are illegal. If you believe you've been retaliated against, contact an attorney immediately — retaliation claims have their own separate legal remedies.

items.question: Do I have to use my employer's doctor?
items.answer: In a non-emergency, yes — initially. Georgia employers can maintain a panel of authorized physicians, and you're generally required to seek treatment from that panel. However, you have the right to request a one-time change of physician within the panel. If the panel doctor is not adequately treating your injury, an attorney can challenge the insurer's medical decisions and request an independent medical examination.

items.question: How long do I have to file a workers' comp claim in Georgia?
items.answer: You must report your injury to your employer within 30 days of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80). After that, you have one year from the date of injury to file a formal claim with the State Board of Workers' Compensation (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). Both deadlines matter — missing the 30-day reporting requirement alone can forfeit your benefits entirely.

items.question: Can I also file a personal injury lawsuit if I was hurt at work?
items.answer: In most cases, you cannot sue your employer directly — workers' comp is the exclusive remedy against your employer. However, if a third party contributed to your injury, you can file a personal injury lawsuit against them in addition to your workers' comp claim. Common third parties include contractors, vehicle drivers, equipment manufacturers, and property owners. A third-party claim can recover damages that workers' comp doesn't cover — including pain and suffering and full lost wages.

items.question: What is the difference between temporary and permanent disability benefits in Georgia?
items.answer: Temporary total disability (TTD) pays two-thirds of your average weekly wage while you're completely unable to work, up to the state maximum. Temporary partial disability (TPD) applies when you return to modified duty at lower pay. Permanent partial disability (PPD) provides a scheduled number of weeks of benefits based on the body part affected and your impairment rating. Permanent total disability (PTD) provides extended benefits for workers who can never return to any form of work.

items.question: What happens if my work injury gets worse over time?
items.answer: If your condition worsens after a settlement or award, Georgia allows you to request additional benefits in certain circumstances — particularly for medical treatment. However, if you accepted a full and final settlement that closed out your medical benefits, your options may be limited. This is exactly why you should never accept a final settlement without an attorney reviewing it first.

betterWay.heading: A Better Way to Find the Right Personal
betterWay.body:
Accident Professionals is not a law firm. We are a nationwide network that helps injured people connect with vetted personal injury attorneys and receive support during the early stages of the process.

For injured clients, that means you are not left searching through random law firm ads or wondering who to call. We learn what happened, where your accident took place, what type of help you need, and whether language preference matters. Then we connect you with an attorney who fits your situation and serves your area.

For attorneys, AP helps organize the front end of the client experience. Our team handles initial intake, gathers key details, supports scheduling, and helps clients stay informed, so your firm receives better-prepared opportunities and can focus on the legal work.

clientFaqs.question: How do Accident Professionals match me with an attorney?
clientFaqs.answer: When you contact us, we gather basic information about your accident, including what happened, where it occurred, and what type of injury or case you may have. We use that information to help connect you with a vetted personal injury attorney who fits your case type, location, and service area.

clientFaqs.question: Does it cost anything to use the Accident Professionals network?
clientFaqs.answer: No. It is free to contact Accident Professionals and be matched with an attorney. The attorneys in our network typically work on a contingency-fee basis, which means you generally do not pay attorney fees unless your case is resolved successfully.

clientFaqs.question: Is Accident Professionals a law firm?
clientFaqs.answer: No. Accident Professionals is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice or representation. We are a network that helps injured people connect with vetted personal injury attorneys and provides support during the early stages of the process.

clientFaqs.question: What if the attorney I'm matched with isn't the right fit?
clientFaqs.answer: If the match is not the right fit, let us know. We can look at your situation again and work to connect you with another attorney in the network who may better suit your case type, location, and preferences.

clientFaqs.question: Can I request a specific attorney I've seen in the directory?
clientFaqs.answer: Yes. If you have seen an attorney in our directory that you would like to work with, you can tell us during intake and we will do our best to connect you, subject to the attorney's availability and case fit.

clientFaqs.question: How is Accident Professionals different from finding a lawyer on my own?
clientFaqs.answer: Instead of searching through random ads and cold-calling firms, AP reviews attorneys before including them, handles your initial intake, gathers key details, and connects you with an attorney who fits your situation — so you spend less time guessing who to call.

attorneyFaqs.question: How do I apply to join the AP attorney network?
attorneyFaqs.answer: Complete the attorney application on this page. Once submitted, our team reviews your bar admission, practice focus, insurance, and service areas. Applications are typically reviewed within 2 business days, and if there is a fit we schedule a short introductory call.

attorneyFaqs.question: What are the requirements to join?
attorneyFaqs.answer: At minimum, we look for active bar admission, personal injury law as your primary practice, professional liability insurance, a clean disciplinary record, and a commitment to responsive client communication.

attorneyFaqs.question: How are clients referred to me?
attorneyFaqs.answer: Clients are pre-screened through our intake process. We verify accident details and establish communication before referral, then connect clients whose case type, location, and language needs match your practice.

attorneyFaqs.question: Is there a fee to participate?
attorneyFaqs.answer: We will review participation details with you during the introductory call. Our focus is on fit and quality, and we will walk you through how the network operates before you join.

attorneyFaqs.question: Do I have to be licensed in Georgia?
attorneyFaqs.answer: AP is expanding nationwide, but we currently focus heavily on Georgia. You should be licensed and in good standing in the states where you intend to accept referred clients.
